title: Hydrometeorological Processes

competencies.text: Describe typhoons, floods, landslides, storm surges, and heat waves.

days.title: Tropical Cyclones
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will describe typhoons, floods, landslides, storm surges and heat waves — their causes, warning signs and effects.

🌀 How a Tropical Cyclone Forms

Tropical cyclones form over warm ocean water (at least about 26.5 °C). Warm, moist air rises, cools and condenses into clouds, releasing heat that fuels more rising air. Earth's rotation makes the system spin — counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. Parts:

  • Eye — calm center with the lowest pressure.
  • Eyewall — ring of the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
  • Rain bands — spiral bands that bring rain far from the center.

📢 PAGASA Tropical Cyclone Wind Signals

SignalWind speed (km/h)Possible impact
No. 139–61Minimal to minor threat
No. 262–88Minor to moderate threat
No. 389–117Moderate to significant threat
No. 4118–184Significant to severe threat
No. 5185 or higherExtreme threat to life and property

Signals describe wind. Heavy rain, floods and storm surges can be dangerous even under a low signal — always read PAGASA's rainfall and storm-surge warnings too.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: What is the main source of energy for a typhoon?

choices.label: Heat from warm ocean water
Cold air from the poles
Lightning inside the clouds
Strong winds over land

scenario.explanation: Warm seawater evaporates; when the vapor condenses into clouds, it releases heat that powers the storm.

scenario.text: Which part of a typhoon has the strongest winds?

choices.label: The eyewall
The calm eye
The outer rain bands
The area far behind it

scenario.explanation: The eyewall surrounding the eye has the most intense winds and heaviest rain.

scenario.text: Why do typhoons usually weaken after crossing land?

choices.label: They lose their warm, moist ocean air
Mountains add more heat to the storm clouds
Land makes the typhoon spin much faster
Cities cool the air until it turns to snow

scenario.explanation: Without warm ocean water to evaporate, the storm loses its energy source; friction with land also slows it.

days.title: Floods, Landslides and Storm Surges
days.content:
🌊 Storm Surge

A storm surge is an abnormal rise of sea level as a strong typhoon approaches the coast. Strong onshore winds pile up water, and low pressure lets the sea bulge upward. Shallow, funnel-shaped bays make it worse. During Super Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan, 2013), storm surges over 5 m flooded Tacloban.

💧 Floods

  • River floods — rivers overflow after days of heavy rain.
  • Flash floods — sudden, fast-rising water within minutes to hours, often in mountain areas or blocked creeks.
  • Urban floods — concrete and clogged drains stop water from soaking in.

⛰️ Landslides

A landslide is the downslope movement of soil, rock and debris. Triggers: long or heavy rain soaking slopes, earthquakes, and removing vegetation or cutting slopes for roads. Warning signs: new cracks on slopes, tilting trees or posts, muddy springs, rumbling sounds.

☀️ Heat Waves

Periods of unusually high temperatures and humidity. PAGASA reports the heat index — what the temperature "feels like" when humidity is included.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each term to its description. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.right: Rotating storm formed over warm ocean water
match.why: Called a typhoon at its strongest levels in our region.

match.right: Calm center with the lowest pressure
match.why: Skies may clear briefly as it passes.

match.right: Ring with the strongest winds and rain
Abnormal sea-level rise pushed ashore by a typhoon
match.why: It caused most deaths in Tacloban during Yolanda.

match.right: Sudden, fast-rising water after intense rain
Downslope movement of soil and rock

match.why: Extreme threat to life and property.

days.title: Warning Signs and Safe Actions
days.content:
🚦 Rainfall Warnings

PAGASA uses a color-coded heavy rainfall warning: Yellow (monitor; flooding possible in low areas), Orange (flooding threatening; be alert for evacuation), Red (serious flooding expected; evacuate low-lying areas).

✅ What to Do

HazardSafe actions
TyphoonSecure the house, prepare a Go Bag, follow evacuation orders before winds become strong
Storm surgeEvacuate coastal areas early to places inland or high enough above the expected surge height
FloodMove to higher ground; never walk or drive through moving floodwater; avoid wading (leptospirosis risk)
LandslideLeave slopes and valleys below them when cracks appear or heavy rain continues
HeatDrink water, rest in shade, avoid strenuous outdoor work at midday

Just 15 cm of fast-moving water can knock a person down, and about 60 cm can float a car.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Choose the safest action. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: PAGASA raises Signal No. 3 over your province. What does this mean?

choices.label: 89–117 km/h winds; moderate to significant threat
Winds of 39–61 km/h; only very light damage
The typhoon has already passed over your whole province
Only boats need to prepare; homes are safe

scenario.explanation: Signal No. 3 means winds of 89–117 km/h are expected — enough to damage houses and topple trees.

scenario.text: Your coastal barangay is warned of a possible 4-meter storm surge. What should residents do?

choices.label: Evacuate early to higher ground inland
Stay home and watch the waves from the shore
Tie the boats closer to the shore and wait
Climb onto the roof once the water arrives

scenario.explanation: Storm surges rise rapidly and are very powerful. Evacuating early before the surge arrives saves lives.

scenario.text: After three days of heavy rain, cracks appear on the slope above your house. What is the SAFEST action?

choices.label: Leave immediately and warn neighbors
Fill the cracks with soil and stay inside
Wait until the rain stops before deciding
Move to the room nearest the slope

scenario.explanation: New cracks are a landslide warning sign. Evacuating at once and alerting others is the safest response.

scenario.text: A river near your home is rising fast after hours of rain, and the road is covered with moving water. What should you do?

choices.label: Go to higher ground; never cross it
Drive across quickly before it gets deeper
Wade through holding a rope for balance
Wait on the riverbank to watch the water

scenario.explanation: Moving floodwater can sweep away people and cars. Seek higher ground instead of crossing.

scenario.text: Why can a weak typhoon (Signal No. 1) still cause deadly floods?

choices.label: It can bring very heavy rain even with weak winds
Weak typhoons always have much stronger storm surges
Signal No. 1 means the typhoon is the strongest
Floods are caused only by wind, not by rain

scenario.explanation: Signals refer to wind. A slow, wet tropical cyclone can drop huge amounts of rain and cause floods and landslides.

days.title: Why the Philippines Is So Exposed
days.content:
🗺️ Exposure Factors

  • Location in the western Pacific typhoon belt with warm seas all year.
  • Long coastlines and many people living in low coastal areas.
  • Steep, deforested mountains that shed rain quickly — floods and landslides.
  • Rapid urban growth with clogged drainage and informal settlements along rivers.

🌡️ Climate Change Links

Warmer seas give typhoons more energy and moisture, so the strongest storms are expected to become more intense and wetter. Rising sea levels make storm surges reach farther inland. Heat waves are becoming more frequent.

🧠 Hazard + Vulnerability = Risk

A typhoon is a hazard. It becomes a disaster when it hits a community that is exposed and vulnerable. Early warnings, strong houses, good drainage, healthy forests and mangroves, and prepared families reduce the risk.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

escape.text: About how many tropical cyclones enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility each year?

choices.label: About 20
About 2
About 5
About 100

escape.explanation: On average about 20 tropical cyclones enter PAR yearly, with several making landfall.

choices.label: Typhoon winds and low pressure piling up seawater
An earthquake suddenly lifting the deep sea floor up high
Heavy rain filling up the ocean from above
The Moon pulling water away from the coast

escape.explanation: Onshore winds pile up water and low air pressure lets the sea rise; together they flood the coast.

escape.text: Which agency issues tropical cyclone wind signals and rainfall warnings?

choices.label: PAGASA
PHIVOLCS
DepEd
DOH

escape.explanation: PAGASA, under DOST, monitors weather and issues typhoon signals, rainfall and heat index advisories.

escape.text: What does the heat index measure?

choices.label: How hot it feels with humidity included
The temperature of the ocean's surface water
The amount of rain in one hour
The wind speed of a typhoon

escape.explanation: Humidity reduces sweat evaporation, so it feels hotter than the air temperature alone.

escape.text: Which human activity MOST increases landslide risk on slopes?

choices.label: Clearing trees from steep hillsides
Planting bamboo along riverbanks
Building drainage canals on slopes
Using terraces for hillside farming

escape.explanation: Tree roots bind soil. Removing them leaves slopes loose and easily saturated.

escape.text: What is the safest response to moving floodwater on a road?

choices.label: Turn back and go to higher ground
Drive through it at a very high speed
Walk through it to save time
Swim across to the other side

escape.explanation: Fast water can knock people down and float vehicles. Avoid entering it altogether.
